title: 7 Best Langfuse Alternatives in 2026 (and What Each One Owns)
summary: Langfuse earned its default status in LLM observability, but the ClickHouse stack, the unit-based bill and the v4 migration push teams to look around. Seven alternatives compared on what each one owns, with facts checked November 22, 2026.
body_markdown:
*Langfuse earned its default status in LLM observability, and plenty of teams should keep it. This list is for the rest: the ClickHouse stack that became a second job, the bill that moves with every judge score, and the v4 migration that started this month. Facts below come from official pages and dated public sources, checked this week. Each entry answers one question most comparisons skip: who owns what after the trace.*


Langfuse is the strongest open-source option for tracing and evaluating LLM applications, and for many teams it is the right default. You end up on a "Langfuse alternatives" page for one of three reasons. You self-host it and the infrastructure got heavier than the product. The usage-based bill moved in a direction you did not expect. Or Langfuse Cloud's v4 cutover on November 16, 2026 just handed you an SDK migration you did not plan for.


One distinction frames the whole list. Every tool on this page, Langfuse included, watches your agent. None of them owns what happens after the trace. The fix and the follow-through stay yours. Some of these tools watch better than Langfuse does. One of them is not a watcher at all.


## TL;DR


- Langfuse stays the default for self-hosted, MIT-licensed tracing. Cloud starts at $29/month for Core, and every trace, observation and score bills as a unit.
- The friction teams report is operational: ClickHouse upkeep on self-hosting, and a bill that grows with trace depth.
- LangSmith fits LangChain deepest and bills $39 per seat plus usage. Self-hosting requires an Enterprise contract.
- Opik and Arize Phoenix are the true open-source alternates, under Apache-2.0 and Elastic License 2.0.
- Every tool here watches. If you want the work owned, the last entry covers that.


## What Langfuse gets right


Start with the credit, because it is real. The core is MIT-licensed, and the free self-hosted distribution includes Enterprise SSO and organization-level RBAC \[1\]. Ingestion is OpenTelemetry-native, and the integration list covers LangChain, LangGraph, the OpenAI SDKs, Vercel AI SDK and more \[2\]. Every paid cloud plan has unlimited users, and on September 30, 2025 Core dropped from $59 to $29 a month \[3\]. Since January 2026 Langfuse belongs to ClickHouse, which puts a serious database company behind the self-hosted store \[4\]. Users notice the polish: one Hacker News commenter called it "by far the best of the langs (-chain, -graph, -smith, -flow) in terms of UI/DX/integration/docs/quality" in January 2026 \[5\]. Production teams back that up. Ramp's engineers described scoring and clustering traces to propose fixes, and reported 10 to 20% fewer tokens and 30% faster sessions on their Research agent \[6\].


Cloud pricing, checked November 22, 2026: Hobby is free with 50,000 units a month, 2 users and 30-day data access. Core is $29/month with 100,000 units included, then $8 per 100,000 units, 90-day data access and unlimited users. Pro is $199/month with 3-year retention plus SOC2 and ISO27001 reports. A Teams add-on with SSO and RBAC costs $300/month on top, and Enterprise is $2,499/month \[1\].


## Where the friction shows up


The bill has a shape worth understanding before you compare plans. A unit is a trace, an observation, or a score \[7\]. Scores from LLM-as-a-judge, annotation queues and experiments count as units too, so the meter runs faster on teams that evaluate in production \[8\]. The plan gap is steep: 90-day data access on Core, 3-year retention at $199 on Pro \[1\].


GILD ran a concrete month through the list prices: a 10-person team producing 200,000 traces, each with 10 observations and one evaluator score. That is 2.4 million Langfuse units, which lands at $199/month on Core or $369 on Pro. The same month costs $1,340 on LangSmith Plus, so Langfuse wins that comparison. The bill does track trace depth, though: at 50 observations per trace, the same traffic reaches about $757 on Langfuse Core while LangSmith stays at $1,340 \[9\]. If cost is your main axis, we published our own numbers on[why per-seat pricing is about to break](https://www.vybe.build/blog/ai-agent-cost-per-seat-pricing-breaking) and[how we cut our AI agent bill](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-cut-your-ai-agent-bill) .


Self-hosting is where the second friction lives. The stack is ClickHouse, Postgres and Redis, not one container \[10\]. GILD read 72 public accounts published between February 2025 and October 2026: 26 of the 30 that say where they run Langfuse self-host it, and 14 of those raise the cost of running ClickHouse and the services around it \[6\]. The issue tracker backs them up. One issue from April 2025 describes ClickHouse spiking CPU while idle \[11\]. A Hacker News commenter noted in January 2026 that the ClickHouse shard in their stack used more memory than headless Chrome \[12\].


Then there is timing. Langfuse Cloud cut over to v4 on November 16, 2026, and teams spent September and October migrating SDKs and APIs ahead of it \[6\]. If that migration just landed on your desk, the alternatives below are worth 20 minutes of your time.


## 1. Vybe: owns the work, not the trace


Disclosure first: we build Vybe, so weigh our entry accordingly.


Vybe is not an observability tool. It is the agent platform the trace would be watching. Agents on Vybe are goal-based: they hold an outcome end to end, run on schedules and triggers, work inside a budget, and keep going until the goal closes or a human steps in. Evals and human review sit in the loop where judgment is needed.


The reason it opens this list: observability tells you an agent went off the rails after the run. Ownership means someone is accountable before the run and for the follow-up after it. We make the case in more depth in[Agents are task-based. They should be goal-based.](https://www.vybe.build/blog/agents-are-task-based-they-should-be-goal-based)


Where Vybe is the wrong fit: if you run a large in-house model stack and need forensic OpenTelemetry depth across thousands of spans, keep Langfuse or Phoenix for that. Vybe does not replace a tracing backend. It removes the need for one to babysit the work.


## 2. LangSmith: owns the LangChain loop


LangSmith is LangChain's observability and eval platform. If your stack is LangChain or LangGraph, it is the most integrated option here: tracing, online and offline evals, prompt hub and playground \[13\].


Pricing is the part to model early. Developer is free with one seat and 5,000 base traces a month. Plus is $39 per seat per month with 10,000 base traces included, then usage in LangChain Standard Units at $1.00 per LSU, with extra traces at 0.005 LSU each, about $5 per 1,000 \[13\]. Self-hosting is Enterprise-only \[13\]. GILD's worked month above costs $1,340 on LangSmith Plus, mostly seats plus per-trace usage \[9\]. Trace debugging is what LangSmith users praise most, per GILD's roundup of 110 public accounts \[14\]. What it does not claim: it does not run your agents, and prompt iteration is manual through the playground.


## 3. Arize Phoenix: owns the lightweight open-source stack


Phoenix is Arize's open-source tracing and evaluation tool, free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0 \[15\]. It is OpenTelemetry-native and small enough that two developers in GILD's research moved to a single Phoenix container from a Langfuse stack \[6\]. A small startup picked it in 2025 as the one tool that worked with OpenTelemetry out of the box \[16\].


The managed side is Arize AX: Free covers 25,000 spans a month with 15-day retention, Pro is $50/month with 50,000 spans and 30-day retention \[15\]. Arize's PXI agent helps debug traces and iterate on prompts. Two caveats: Elastic License 2.0 is source-available rather than OSI open source, which matters to some procurement teams, and GILD's Arize roundup notes that most teams which left Phoenix at production volume moved to Langfuse \[17\].


## 4. Opik (Comet): owns the fix, not just the log


Opik is Comet's open-source observability platform, Apache-2.0, and the self-hosted version runs the same codebase as the hosted one \[18\]. Free cloud covers 25,000 spans a month for up to 10 team members. Pro is $19/month for up to 50 members and 100,000 spans \[18\]. That is the cheapest managed entry on this page.


What makes it distinct: automatic prompt optimization with six algorithms, plus an assistant positioned around getting fixes from traces, not just logs \[18\]. If your goal is trace, then change the prompt without a human rebuild, Opik and Braintrust are the two entries built for it. The trade-off is a smaller ecosystem and community than Langfuse or LangSmith.


## 5. Braintrust: owns the eval loop


Braintrust is evals-first: tracing, datasets, scoring and playgrounds in one place \[19\]. Pricing is a platform fee plus usage, with no per-seat charge: Starter is free with $10 in credits, Pro is a $249/month platform fee plus usage such as $4 per GB of processed data \[19\].


Its Loop agent runs evals, generates test cases and iterates on prompts on its own, which puts it closest to closing the loop from evaluation to change \[19\]. Deployment is SaaS-first, with on-prem or hosted options reserved for Enterprise. If evaluation quality is your bottleneck rather than trace volume, start here.


## 6. Helicone: owns the API boundary


Helicone approaches the problem from the other end: a gateway in front of your model calls. One integration gives you routing, caching, rate limits and fallbacks, plus the observability that comes with sitting on the request path: traces, sessions, cost and latency metrics \[20\].


It is Apache-2.0 open source. Hobby is free up to 10,000 requests a month. Pro is $79/month with unlimited seats \[20\]. The pricing page now carries a banner saying Helicone is part of Experiential Labs, worth knowing before you commit it as infrastructure \[20\]. Limits: the eval and prompt-experiment depth sits behind Langfuse, and a gateway that routes traffic is not an agent orchestrator.


## 7. AgentOps: owns the debugging view


AgentOps focuses on the developer debugging experience: session replay, step-by-step execution graphs, time-travel debugging and cost tracking for agent runs, with prompt-injection detection among its checks \[21\]. The app is MIT-licensed open source. Basic is free up to 5,000 events, and Pro starts at $40/month on a pay-as-you-go basis \[21\].


It is monitoring-first: the eval depth of Langfuse or Braintrust is not the pitch. If your problem is seeing what the agent did and why, it is the most direct tool here.


## Also on our radar


Three more, verified this week. LangWatch bundles red-teaming and governance with observability, with a Growth plan at $34 per core seat/month and 200,000 events included \[22\]. W&B Weave now ships under the CoreWeave Forge brand after Weights & Biases was folded into CoreWeave, with Pro starting at $60/month \[23\]. PostHog renamed its LLM observability to AI Observability and includes 100,000 events a month free with unlimited team members \[24\].


## How to choose


GILD's advice is to measure four numbers before comparing any plans: traces per month from a week of production traffic, observations and scores per trace, the share of traces that need extended retention, and the number of people who need to read traces \[9\]. On unit-billed tools, the second number moves the bill more than the plan tier does.


Match the tool to the gap you need to close:


- Traces must stay in your network and you can staff the ClickHouse work: Langfuse self-host, or Opik for an Apache-2.0 license. Want the smallest footprint: Phoenix.
- Your stack is LangChain or LangGraph: LangSmith, and model the seats before the trace volume.
- Cheapest managed start: Opik's free cloud tier, or PostHog's 100,000 free events.
- The problem is cost and latency control at the model API: Helicone.
- You debug agent behavior like software: AgentOps.
- You want evals to end in prompt changes without a rebuild: Braintrust or Opik.
- You want the outcome owned, not watched: that is a platform decision, and it is the first entry.


If I had to pick one default for a small team starting today, it would be Opik: Apache-2.0, a free managed tier, and $19 a month when you outgrow it. If you already run Langfuse and it works, none of this is urgent. The evals side deserves its own homework before you commit; our guide on[how to evaluate an AI agent](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-evaluate-ai-agents) covers what a real eval looks like, and[our CodeRabbit alternatives comparison](https://www.vybe.build/blog/best-coderabbit-alternatives) applies the same what-it-does-versus-what-it-owns lens to code review tools.


## FAQ


### Is Langfuse free?


Self-hosting is free under MIT for the core product, and the ee/ folders need a license key. Langfuse Cloud has a free Hobby plan with 50,000 units a month, 2 users and 30-day data access. Paid cloud starts at $29/month \[1\].


### What changed in Langfuse's pricing?


Per-seat Pro billing arrived in late 2024, with the pull request that introduced it merged in December 2024 \[25\]. A Hacker News commenter still described Langfuse as seat-billed in August 2025 \[26\]. On September 30, 2025 the company cut Core from $59 to $29, and its monetization handbook, last updated September 7, 2026, states that it does not price on seats \[3\]. Today every trace, observation and score bills as a unit.


### Does Langfuse run my agents?


No. It traces and evaluates whichever runtime you pick, and its own comparison pages state that it sells no runtime or framework \[2\]. Orchestration stays in your code, which is why the trace alone does not fix anything.


### What is the best free alternative to Langfuse?


For self-hosting, Opik under Apache-2.0 and Arize Phoenix under Elastic License 2.0 are both free \[15\] \[18\]. For a managed free tier, Opik's cloud covers 25,000 spans a month and PostHog's AI Observability includes 100,000 events a month \[18\] \[24\].


## The trace is not the fix


Most teams searching this query are debugging agents by hand: read the trace, change the prompt, rerun, repeat. The tools above make that loop faster, and Langfuse does it best among them. We build Vybe because we think the loop itself is the problem. An agent that owns an outcome carries its schedule, budget and follow-through, and asks for review when judgment is needed, instead of waiting for a human to read a trace and act.


If you are shopping for a trace viewer, the entries above should get you there. If you are shopping for someone to own the outcome,[try Vybe free](https://www.vybe.build/) and put one agent on a real goal this week. You can also browse[what teams have built in the gallery](https://www.vybe.build/gallery) .
